rules: Show ONLY the text written in each scene. Never add filler text, quotes, slogans or labels that are not in this file.
Each scene appears when its 'say' line starts and stays until the next scene.
Nothing may overlap. Every item must be fully visible inside the board.
Sticky notes only appear when a scene has a 'sticky' field.

Cosmo lines: 'cosmoBefore' is spoken by Cosmo before the scene's 'say'; 'cosmoAfter' is spoken by Cosmo after the scene's last Astra line ('sayAfter' if present, else 'say'). Only the speaking character shows in the slot.

Every scene's board content (question, choices, table, passage, cards, steps) must be fully visible on screen for the whole time that scene's lines are spoken, including during the chat countdown and after the reveal.

scenes.title: The ACT Crash Course
scenes.subtitle: + 3 quick wins & insider tips
scenes.say: Hey everyone! I'm Astra, the AI tutor here at Aced. Welcome to our first live lesson! Tonight is your ACT crash course: how the test works, how it's scored, and three quick wins you can use right away. When a practice question pops up, type your answer in the Zoom chat before I reveal it. And drop any questions in the chat too. We'll answer them after the lesson. Let's get started.
scenes.cosmoAfter: Hi, I'm Cosmo! I'm studying for the ACT too, so I'll ask the questions you're probably thinking.

scenes.title: What's on the test
scenes.say: Thanks, Cosmo! Let's start with the big picture. The ACT has three main sections: English, Math, and Reading. Science and Writing are optional.

First, English. Fifty questions in thirty-five minutes. You'll edit short passages for grammar, punctuation, and how ideas flow. Second, Math. Forty-five questions in fifty minutes. Algebra, functions, geometry, and statistics. And yes, you can use an approved calculator. Third, Reading. Thirty-six questions in forty minutes. You'll answer questions about details, main ideas, and what the author means. Some questions compare two short passages. And then there's Science. Forty questions in forty minutes. It's optional, and it's mostly about reading graphs, tables, and experiments. There's also an optional essay, called Writing.

scenes.caption: 4 answer choices. Every question.
scenes.say: One more thing. Every multiple choice question now has four answer choices, including Math. Keep that in mind. It matters for scoring.

scenes.title: How it's scored
scenes.say: Now, scoring. Each section gets a score from one to thirty-six.
scenes.cosmoAfter: Wait, so does Science count toward my main score?

scenes.say: Good question. No. Your composite score, the big number colleges look at, is the average of English, Math, and Reading, rounded to the nearest whole number. If you take Science, you get a separate Science score.
So if you get a twenty-four in English, a twenty-six in Math, and a twenty-five in Reading, that adds up to seventy-five. Divide by three, and your composite is twenty-five.

scenes.caption: Wrong answer = blank answer = 0 points.
scenes.say: Here's the most important rule on the whole test. There's no penalty for wrong answers. A wrong answer and a blank answer both earn zero. So never leave a question blank. If you're stuck, cross out the choices you know are wrong, pick your best answer, and move on.

scenes.question: 30 seconds left, 5 questions to go. What do you do?
scenes.answer: Fill in an answer for every one.
scenes.explain: Answer what you can quickly. Never leave a blank.
scenes.say: Quick check! In the chat: you have thirty seconds left and five questions you haven't answered. What should you do?
scenes.sayAfter: Make sure all five have an answer before time runs out. If one looks quick, solve it. But don't leave any blank. With four choices, even a guess has a chance. A blank has none.

scenes.say: Let's talk timing, because running out of time costs students a lot of points. In English, you get about forty-two seconds per question. In Math and Reading, about sixty-seven seconds. And in Science, about one minute. Those are averages. Some questions take ten seconds. Others take longer.
scenes.cosmoAfter: Forty-two seconds? What if I'm still stuck after a minute?

scenes.caption: Best guess · mark it · move on.
scenes.sticky: One hard question shouldn't steal time from three easy ones.
scenes.say: Then ask yourself one thing: am I making progress? If you're close, a little more time is worth it. But if you're staring at it with no next step, make your best guess, mark it, and move on. Come back at the end if there's time. One hard question shouldn't steal time from three easy ones.

scenes.title: Comma after an intro phrase
scenes.say: Okay, quick win number one. This one's for English. When a sentence starts with an intro phrase, like 'After the game,' you usually put a comma right after it.

scenes.title: Lift it out. Still a sentence?
scenes.check: "We got pizza." ✓ full sentence → comma after the intro phrase
scenes.say: Here's a quick check. Lift the intro phrase out. If what's left is a full sentence, like 'We got pizza,' the intro phrase is separate from the main sentence, so it gets a comma.
scenes.cosmoAfter: So does every word at the start of a sentence get a comma?

scenes.explain: Semicolons and colons need a full sentence before them.
scenes.say: Not always. Let's test it. Your turn! In the chat: which is correct?
scenes.sayAfter: It's B! 'Afterward' is an intro word, so a comma separates it from the main sentence. And semicolons and colons need a full sentence before them. 'Afterward' isn't a full sentence, so C and D are out.

choices: Running every morning, helps me focus.
Running every morning helps me focus.
Running, every morning helps me focus.
Running every morning; helps me focus.
scenes.explain: "Running every morning" is the subject. No comma between a subject and its verb.
scenes.say: Now watch for a comma that doesn't belong. Which is correct?
scenes.sayAfter: It's B! Lift out 'Running every morning,' and you're left with 'helps me focus.' That's not a full sentence. Here, 'Running every morning' isn't an intro phrase. It's the subject. And we don't put a comma between a subject and its verb.

scenes.caption: A period and a semicolon can both join two full sentences. Check structure and meaning.
scenes.say: Here's a tip. Fancy punctuation isn't automatically right. A period and a semicolon can both join two full sentences. So don't pick an answer because it looks more advanced. Check the sentence structure and the meaning.

scenes.caption: If cutting keeps the meaning, it's often the best answer.
scenes.say: Next, wordiness. The ACT likes writing that's clear and doesn't repeat itself. If a choice cuts words, ask: does the sentence keep its meaning and stay clear? If yes, that's often the best answer.

scenes.stem: She returned back to the classroom. Which is best?
scenes.explain: "Returned" already means "went back." Clear and no repeats.
scenes.say: Let's try it. She returned back to the classroom. Which choice is best? Chat it in!
scenes.sayAfter: It's B, 'returned to.' 'Returned' already means 'went back,' so 'back' repeats the same idea. We're not picking it just because it's shorter. We're picking it because it's clearer and means the same thing.

scenes.caption: Test the answer choices in the problem.
scenes.say: Quick win number two is for Math. If you get stuck setting up an equation, try working backward. Plug the answer choices into the problem and see which one works.
Try this one in the chat. If three x plus five equals twenty, what is x?
scenes.sayAfter: It's B, five! You can solve it: subtract five to get three x equals fifteen, then divide by three. Or plug in: three times five is fifteen, plus five is twenty. Both ways work.

scenes.work: Try B: 2(7) − 7 = 7 → too small ↑   Try C: 2(9) − 7 = 11 ✓
scenes.say: Now let's plug in. Two x minus seven equals eleven. What is x? Try the choices, and put your answer in the chat.
scenes.sayAfter: It's C, nine! When the choices go from small to big, starting in the middle can save time. Try B, seven. Two times seven is fourteen, minus seven is seven. Too small, and since this gets bigger as x gets bigger, go bigger. Try C, nine. Two times nine is eighteen, minus seven is eleven. That's it!
scenes.sticky: Ordered choices? Start in the middle ↕
scenes.cosmoAfter: So I don't always have to solve the equation first?

scenes.say: Right. Use whichever way is faster for that problem. Now, here's a trap the ACT loves. If two x equals ten, what is x plus three? Careful! Chat your answer.
scenes.sayAfter: It's B, eight! Two x equals ten, so x is five. But the question asks for x plus three, which is eight. Five is sitting right there as choice A to catch people who stop too early. Always check what the last line is asking for.
scenes.cosmoAfter: Okay, I definitely would have picked five.

scenes.title: Letters in the answers? Pick a number.
steps: Pick an easy number that fits the rules (like n = 2)
Plug it into the question and each choice
Two choices match? Try another number
scenes.say: You're not alone, Cosmo. That's why we practice! One more Math tip. When the answer choices have letters in them, like n or x, you can pick your own number. If the question says n is even, try n equals two. Just make sure your number follows every rule in the question. And if two choices both work, try a second number.

scenes.big: If you can't point to it, don't pick it.
scenes.caption: Said directly or strongly implied, the passage backs it up.
scenes.say: Quick win number three is for Reading. The right answer is always backed up by the passage. Not your opinion, and not just what sounds smart. Sometimes it's said directly, and sometimes you have to infer it. But either way, you should be able to point to the words that support it.
So before you look at the choices, find the lines in the passage, and predict the answer in your own words. Then pick the choice that matches.

scenes.title: Watch out for answers that are…
items: True, but don't answer the question
scenes.say: Wrong answers usually do one of three things. They're too extreme, with words like 'always' or 'never' that the passage doesn't support. They're true, but don't answer the question. Or they mix up details from different parts of the passage.

scenes.passage: Maya had practiced the solo for weeks. But when the spotlight hit her, her hands shook. She closed her eyes, counted to three, and began to play.
scenes.stem: Which choice is best supported by the passage?
choices: Maya had never played the solo before.
Maya was nervous when she started to perform.
Maya's solo was the best in the show.
scenes.explain: A is contradicted · C is too extreme · D is never said.
scenes.say: Your turn! Read this short passage. Which choice is best supported?
scenes.sayAfter: It's B! Point to the proof: 'her hands shook.' That supports that she was nervous. A doesn't fit, because she practiced for weeks. C says 'always,' which is too broad for one moment. And D is never mentioned. We used a real detail from the text to back up our answer.

scenes.caption: Start with a passage type you're strong at. Then keep moving.
scenes.say: A Reading tip. You don't have to do the passages in order. If one type is easier for you, you can start there. Just don't spend long deciding, and make sure your answers go in the right spots.

scenes.title: Paired passages: one at a time
steps: Read Passage A → answer its questions
Read Passage B → answer its questions
Then answer the questions about both
scenes.say: For the paired passages, try this. Read Passage A, and answer only its questions. Then read Passage B, and answer its questions. Save the questions about both for last. It keeps the two authors' ideas separate.

scenes.caption: Most Science questions are about graphs, tables, and experiments.
scenes.say: Some science knowledge can help, but most Science questions are about reading data: graphs, tables, and experiments. So start by figuring out what the question asks and where the data is.
scenes.cosmoBefore: Science worries me. Do I need to memorize a lot of biology and chemistry?

scenes.stem: If growth changes steadily, about how much would a plant grow with 10 hours of light?
scenes.work: 10 hours is between 8 and 12 → growth is between 6 and 9 cm → 7.5 cm ✓
scenes.say: Look at this table. It shows how much a plant grows with different hours of light each day. If growth changes steadily between eight and twelve hours, about how much would it grow with ten hours? Answer in the chat!
scenes.sayAfter: It's B, seven and a half centimeters! Ten hours is halfway between eight and twelve. So we estimate growth halfway between six and nine centimeters. That's seven and a half. We're estimating between two data points, using only the table.

scenes.caption: If it points to a figure or table, go straight there.
scenes.say: Science tip number one. For data questions, read the question first. If it points you to a figure or table, go straight there. If it asks about an experiment's purpose, you may need to read more of the setup.

scenes.title: Before you answer, check:
items: The units (cm vs. mm, seconds vs. minutes)
scenes.say: Tip number two. Before you answer a chart question, check three things: the labels on the axes, the units, and the key. A lot of wrong answers use the right number with the wrong units.

scenes.caption: Write each scientist's main idea in 3–4 words.
scenes.say: And tip number three. Some passages compare scientists who disagree. As you read each one, write their main idea in a few words, like 'Scientist one: temperature matters.' Then it's much easier to see where they agree and disagree.

scenes.stem: 2 minutes left. 4 English questions to go. What's your best move?
choices: Spend it all on the first question
Answer the quick ones, then make sure all have an answer
Go back and check old answers
scenes.explain: Protect the points you can still earn. Never leave a blank.
scenes.say: Last question! You have two minutes left in English and four questions to go. What's your best move?
scenes.sayAfter: It's C! Answer the quick ones first. If one takes too long, make your best guess and move on. Before time runs out, make sure all four have an answer.

scenes.title: Use two passes
steps: Pass 1: answer every question you're sure about
Mark anything that takes too long and keep moving
Pass 2: go back to the marked ones with the time left
scenes.sticky: Halfway through the time? Aim to be halfway through the questions.
scenes.say: One last strategy: two passes. On your first pass, answer the questions you can do without getting stuck, and mark the hard ones. On your second pass, go back to the marked ones. And here's a checkpoint: when half the time is gone, try to be about halfway through the questions. Practice this before test day so it feels natural.

scenes.title: Tonight's 5 stars
items: Back it up with the passage
scenes.say: Let's put it all together. Know your timing. Never leave a blank. Use the lift-out check for commas. Try plugging in answer choices in Math. And in Reading, back up your answer with the passage. Every one of these is a skill on your Aced star map, and your stars get brighter as you practice.

scenes.title: See you next Sunday ✦
scenes.say: That's it for tonight! Head to your star map on Aced and pick a skill to practice. If you want a full ACT-style practice test, the Aced Mock Test is on Saturday, December fifth. And next Sunday at five, we're going deeper into commas: when you need one, when you don't, and the traps to watch for. See you next week!
scenes.cosmoAfter: Thanks, Astra! I'm going to go practice my commas.
